en: So you can use Bun for managing your
dependencies in your project, but you can
also use it to kind of manage the project
itself. Specifically, you can, for example,
add scripts which you can then execute with
help of Bun.
You probably already know that feature from
Node.js apps. It's not Bun-specific, but in
those scripts, I am now using Bun for doing
different things. For example, we got this
dev script here
where we run the index.ts file. You may
remember that I did that manually before
like this. Well, if we run this frequently,
we can of course wrap it in a script and we
use the special
--watch feature here, which is offered by
Bun,
which does what the name implies. It watches
a file and the files used by that file, the
files imported into that file. And if any of
those files changes, the server is updated
automatically so that you don't have to
restart it manually just to show those
latest changes. Changes.
You also may notice that there is no run in
here. It's just bun,
then this flag, and then the path, because
indeed you can also execute files and
scripts just like this without run.
If you do add run though, you get
autocompletion.
So if I type bun source slash and I hit Tab,
I get nothing.
If I type bun run source slash and I hit
Tab, I get autocompletion. That's one reason
for using Run, at least at the point of time
where I'm recording this.
Now, since we have those scripts here, we
can also run those instead of typing these
commands manually. So I can invoke a script
by running Bun and then the script name like
dev or bun run again. If I hit Tab here, I
get nice autocompletion and I see all the
things I could run, all the scripts I can
run, for example.
And for example, I can run the dev script to
start that dev server but now in watch mode.
So if we were to make any changes to the
code, it would reload and restart
automatically.
There also is
--hot for a hot reload, which does to try to
do the same, watching and reloading, but
unlike watch, it doesn't restart the server,
losing your state, but instead it tries to
just inject the new code into the running
server. Doesn't always work, but something
worth knowing.
Now, besides the watch mode here and my
normal start script, which is exactly the
same command I ran manually before,
You'll also notice that there is a build
script because as mentioned, Bun is also a
build tool and bundler. You can use it to
optimize code for production, to compile
your TypeScript code to JavaScript, for
example, so that this
on-the-fly compilation doesn't have to
happen and could therefore give you another
performance boost.
And you use those build tool and bundler
capabilities by running bun build. Build,
and then some configuration flags, and then
the file you wanna build. And if that file
imports other files, all those files are of
course built and bundled together.
So in my case here, I'm targeting the source
index.ts file,
which does import Svelte here. It's a
dependency I added off screen. It's a type
checking dependency, has nothing to do with
Bun.
And I'm importing index.html. And if we
build the index.ts file,
those packages of course also get optimized
and bundled into the final output.
Now, when running Bun build, you can specify
a target which allows you to configure for
which target you wanna build. So Bun would
build a
Bun application that can use all the Bun
features but wouldn't run in the browser,
for example. If you were building a
client-side application, your target should
be browser.
If you know that you're actually building a
Node.js application that you plan on running
with Node.js but you wanna use Bun as a
build tool, you can also set the target to
Node.
Here the target is Bun because this is a
server-side application that does use Bun
features like bun serve and won't run in the
browser.
So the target is set to Bun,
--production ensures that the code is
optimized and improved as much as possible.
And then you can also set an output
directory with outDir, which simply sets up
the directory the optimized files will be
output in.
And if you would then run this script here,
so the build script here,
or you would run this command manually in
the command line, of course, you'll see
it'll do that. It'll build that program
and it added a dist folder here for me with
an index.js file. And that index.js file has
the
JavaScript code in there.
So that includes that Svelte code which
we're using, but then also the HTML template
all in that JavaScript file and then my
actual Bun code down here, bun serve and so
on. That is my Bun code but you see it's all
heavily optimized to be as small as possible
with the variable names shortened and with
it all being in one line essentially down
here.
And therefore, you cannot just use Bun to
use Bun features in your code or to use it
for package management but also to build and
optimize your program.
